question: David is researching an Earth-like exoplanet near the constellation of Bootes, orbiting a star twice the mass of our Sun. On March 14, 2025, the planet was observed at 3 AU from its parent star. After some time, David observes it again and finds that it has already passed its farthest point from the star and is now at 4 AU . If the planet is known to have a period of 5 years and an eccentricity of 0.5 , what is the shortest amount of time that could have passed since the first observation on March 14, 2025? Assume that David views the orbit face-on and that the exoplanet's velocity component along the semimajor axis has opposite sign at the two observation points.
answer: First, we need to find the planet's semi-major axis through the Kepler's third law. $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{a^{3}}{T^{2}} & =M a & =\sqrt[3]{M T^{2}}=\sqrt[3]{2 \times 5^{2}} & \approx 3.684 \mathrm{AU} \quad[\mathbf{2} \text { points }] \end{aligned} $$ Next, let's find the true anomaly at 3 AU and at 4 AU . This is to give the position of the planet in the ellipse orbit. Remember that when the planet is at 3 AU , it is before the planet passes its farthest distance to its parent star, i.e. its true anomaly must be between $0^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$. This also means that the true anomaly when the planet is at 4 AU must be between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$ since it has passed its farthest distance. $$ \begin{aligned} r & =\frac{a\left(1-e^{2}\right)}{1+e \cos f} \cos f & =\frac{1}{e}\left(\frac{a\left(1-e^{2}\right)}{r}-1\right) f_{3 \mathrm{AU}} & =99^{\circ} 5^{\prime} 27^{\prime \prime} f_{4 \mathrm{AU}} & =231^{\circ} 47^{\prime} 36^{\prime \prime} \quad[\mathbf{3} \text { points }] \end{aligned} $$ From the true anomaly, we must convert it to eccentric anomaly. Similar to before, the eccentric anomaly when the planet is at 3 AU must be between $0^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$ and the eccentric anomaly when the planet is at 4 AU must be between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$. $$ \begin{aligned} \cos E & =\frac{e+\cos f}{1+e \cos f} E_{3 \mathrm{AU}} & =68^{\circ} 12^{\prime} 7.2^{\prime \prime} E_{4 \mathrm{AU}} & =260^{\circ} 7^{\prime} 18.9^{\prime \prime} \quad[4 \text { points }] \end{aligned} $$ From the eccentric anomaly, we must convert it to mean anomaly. Similar to before, the mean anomaly when the planet is at 3 AU must be between 0 and $\pi$ and the mean anomaly when the planet is at 4 AU must be between $\pi$ and $2 \pi$. (The calculation below is in radians) $$ \begin{aligned} M & =E-e \sin E M_{3 \mathrm{AU}} & =0.7261 \mathrm{rad} M_{4 \mathrm{AU}} & =5.0326 \mathrm{rad} \quad[4 \text { points }] \end{aligned} $$ From the mean anomaly, we can find the elapsed time since March 14, 2025. $$ \begin{aligned} M & =\frac{2 \pi}{T} \times\left(t-t_{0}\right) \Delta M & =\frac{2 \pi}{T} \Delta t \Delta t & =\Delta M \times \frac{T}{2 \pi} & =\left(M_{4} \mathrm{AU}-M_{3} \mathrm{AU}\right) \times \frac{5 \mathrm{yrs}}{2 \pi} \Delta t & \approx 3.427 \text { years } \quad[2 \text { points }] \end{aligned} $$
caption: Face-on diagram of the exoplanet's elliptical orbit and observation points.

question: Derive the limiting magnitude for naked-eye visibility of a star in a dark-sky environment, by considering an analogy to a CCD camera. Assume that the dominant noise source is $\sqrt{n}$ photon shot noise, and "visibility" requires a signal-to-noise ratio $(\mathrm{SNR})>1$. You'll need the following information: The dark-adapted human pupil dilates to an aperture of 6 mm . The quantum efficiency of the rod cells used for night vision is around 5\% (averaged across the full visible spectrum), and the effective "exposure time" is roughly 30 ms . For a convenient magnitude reference, the intensity of sunlight within the visible spectrum is $5 \times$ $10^{2} \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$, and the apparent magnitude of the Sun is -26.7 . Feel free to approximate all the visible photons as having wavelength $\lambda=500 \mathrm{~nm}$, for the purpose of calculating the photon energy. This is near the peak sensitivity for human night vision.
answer: The full expression for the signal-to-noise ratio in a CCD camera is $$ \mathrm{SNR}=\frac{I Q t}{\sqrt{I Q t+N_{d} t+N_{r}^{2}}} $$ where $I$ is the photon flux, $Q$ is the quantum efficiency, $t$ is the integration time, and $N_{d}$ and $N_{r}$ are the dark current and read noise. For simplicity we are discarding other sources of noise here (though something like "dark current" does exist in the eye, just close your eyes in a dark room to see it!) The expression just simplifies to the photon shot noise expression: $\mathrm{SNR}=\sqrt{n}=\sqrt{I Q t}$. Given $Q=0.05$ and $t=0.03 \mathrm{~s}$, we need $I=6.7 \times 10^{2}$ photons/sec to achieve $\mathrm{SNR}=1$. For $\lambda=500 \mathrm{~nm}$ photons this intensity $I$ corresponds to a power of $I \frac{h c}{\lambda}=2.6 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~W}$. Since this is the power entering the pupil, the corresponding flux is $$ F_{\text {limit }}=\frac{2.6 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~W}}{\pi(3 \mathrm{~mm})^{2}}=9 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} $$ Finally, we need to convert this to an apparent magnitude. We can use the Sun's apparent magnitude and flux as a reference: $$ M_{\text {limit }}=M_{\odot}-2.5 \log _{10} \frac{F_{\text {limit }}}{F_{\odot}}=-26.7-2.5 \log _{10} \frac{9 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{m}^{2}}{5 \times 10^{2} \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{m}^{2}}=7.7 $$ In reality, the limiting magnitude for pristine dark skies is roughly 6 to 7, with the exact value depending on the observer and the weather conditions. We got pretty close to the right answer!

question: Consider a hypothetical solar sail that starts its trajectory just outside the surface of the Sun and aims to reach Jupiter's orbit. This is a square sail with a size length of $l=50 \mathrm{~m}$, a mass of $m=2.0 \mathrm{~kg}$, and a reflectivity of $\eta=85 \%$. The remaining $15 \%$ of the photons are absorbed by the sail. In order to simplify the calculations, only take into account the gravity and radiation pressure from the Sun, and assume that the sail is initially stationary with respect to the Sun. Estimate how long it would take for this sail to reach Jupiter's orbit. Feel free to make reasonable approximations if needed, but be sure to state and justify any approximations you make.
answer: The radiation pressure is a result of the momentum of the photons, which is given by the following expression: $$ p=\frac{E}{c} $$ Where $p$ corresponds to the momentum, $E$ is the energy of the photon, and $c$ is the speed of light. Since the momentum is conserved after the collision of the photons with the sail, it is possible to write the following expression for the radiation pressure on the sail: $$ P_{r}=(1+\eta) \frac{F_{\odot}}{c} $$ Where $P_{r}$ is the radiation pressure and $F_{\odot}$ is the Solar flux. Note that the $1+\eta$ term comes from the fact that a fraction $\eta$ of the photons being reflected causes a momentum in the opposite direction to their motion before the collision with the sail. In order to preserve the momentum, the sail needs to end up with $1+\eta$ times the initial momentum to account for the reflected photons. Taking into account both the radiation pressure and the gravity, it is possible to find an expression for the acceleration $a$ as a function of the distance $r$ to the Sun: $$ \begin{gathered} m a=(1+\eta) A \frac{F_{\odot}}{c}-\frac{G M_{\odot} m}{r^{2}} m a=(1+\eta) l^{2} \frac{L_{\odot}}{4 \pi r^{2} c}-\frac{G M_{\odot} m}{r^{2}} a=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\left(\frac{(1+\eta) l^{2} L_{\odot}}{4 \pi c m}-G M_{\odot}\right) \end{gathered} $$ In order to simplify the notation, it is convenient to define a term containing all constants on this expression: $k=\frac{(1+\eta) l^{2} L_{\odot}}{4 \pi c m}-G M_{\odot}=\frac{(1+0.85) \cdot 50^{2} \cdot 3.827 \cdot 10^{26}}{4 \pi \cdot 2.998 \cdot 10^{8} \cdot 2.0}-6.674 \cdot 10^{-11} \cdot 1.989 \cdot 10^{30}=1.0 \cdot 10^{20} \mathrm{~m}^{3} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ Using the definition of acceleration and the chain rule: $$ a=\frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{~d} t}=\frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{~d} r} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{~d} r}{\mathrm{~d} t}=v \frac{\mathrm{~d} v}{\mathrm{~d} r} \longrightarrow \frac{k}{r^{2}}=v \frac{\mathrm{~d} v}{\mathrm{~d} r} \longrightarrow \frac{k}{r^{2}} \mathrm{~d} r=v \mathrm{~d} v $$ Integrating to find the velocity of the sail: $$ \begin{aligned} & \int_{R_{\odot}}^{r} \frac{k}{u^{2}} \mathrm{~d} u=\int_{0}^{v} v \mathrm{~d} v & \frac{v^{2}}{2}=k\left(\frac{1}{R_{\odot}}-\frac{1}{r}\right) & v=\sqrt{2 k\left(\frac{1}{R_{\odot}}-\frac{1}{r}\right)} \end{aligned} $$ Since the radius of Jupiter's orbit is much larger than the the radius of the Sun, for most of the trajectory, the velocity of the sail is approximately the following: $$ v \approx \sqrt{\frac{2 k}{R_{\odot}}}=5.4 \cdot 10^{5} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$ This is because the term $\frac{1}{r}$ is negligible compared to $\frac{1}{R_{\odot}}$ for most of the trajectory. Therefore, it is possible to estimate the time to travel to Jupiter as follows: $$ \Delta t \approx \frac{a_{4}}{v}=\frac{5.2 \cdot 1.496 \cdot 10^{11}}{5.4 \cdot 10^{5}}=1.4 \cdot 10^{6} s=16 \text { days. } $$ Answers within one day of this result are acceptable.

question: In a binary neutron star system, two identical neutron stars of mass $M$ each undergo a circular orbit of radius $R$ around their center of mass. This problem explores the general relativistic effect of gravitational waves on this system, but the system can be approximated as Newtonian circular orbits which radiate energy but remain very nearly circular even though the radius is changing very slowly over time. The total gravitational wave luminosity of the system, $L_{G W}$, can be approximated according to general relativity by a single term which includes only a dimensionless constant, the physical constants $G$ and $c$, and $M$ and $R$. Furthermore, $c$ and $R$ are raised to the same power. Using the fact that the dimensionless constant from general relativistic calculations is $\frac{2}{5}$, determine the expression for $L_{G W}$. Use the given value of the dimensionless constant for the remainder of this problem.
answer: $L_{G W}$ has dimensions of energy per time, or $\frac{[M][L]^{2}}{[T]^{3}}$, where $[M]$ is mass, $[L]$ is length, and $[T]$ is time. $G$ has dimensions $\frac{[L]^{3}}{[M][T]^{2}}, c$ has $\frac{[L]}{[T]}, M$ has $[M]$ and $R$ has $[L]$. According to the problem statement, $$ L_{G W}=\frac{2}{5} G^{\alpha}(c R)^{\beta} M^{\gamma}(\mathbf{1} \text { point }), $$ where $\alpha$ through $\delta$ are powers to be determined. This gives the following system of equations to be solved: (2 points) For $[M]: 1=-\alpha+\gamma$, so $\gamma=1+\alpha$; For $[L]: 2=3 \alpha+2 \beta$; For $[T]:-3=-2 \alpha-\beta$. Adding twice the equation for $[T]$ to that for $[L]$ gives $-4=-\alpha$ so $\alpha=4, \beta=-5$, and $\gamma=5$ (1 point). Thus, we have $$ L_{G W}=\frac{2 G^{4} M^{5}}{5 R^{5} c^{5}} \quad(1 \text { point }) . $$

question: In a binary neutron star system, two identical neutron stars of mass $M$ each undergo a circular orbit of radius $R$ around their center of mass. This problem explores the general relativistic effect of gravitational waves on this system, but the system can be approximated as Newtonian circular orbits which radiate energy but remain very nearly circular even though the radius is changing very slowly over time. ( $\mathbf{5}$ points) Using the expression from part (a), find an expression for $\frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{~d} t}$, the rate of change of the radius $R$ of the circular orbit with respect to time, using the same constants and variables. Hint: $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\left(x^{\alpha}\right)=\alpha x^{\alpha-1} \frac{\mathrm{~d} x}{\mathrm{~d} t}$.
answer: According to the virial theorem or the vis-viva equation, the total energy of a circular orbit of masses $M$ and $m$ with $a$ as the distance between the masses is $E=-\frac{G M m}{2 a}$ (2 points). In this case, $m=M$ and $a=2 R$ so $E=-\frac{G M^{2}}{4 R}$. $L_{G W}=-\frac{\mathrm{d} E}{\mathrm{~d} t}=-\frac{G M^{2}}{4 R^{2}} \frac{\mathrm{~d} R}{\mathrm{~d} t}$ (2 points), so $\frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{~d} t}=-\frac{4 R^{2}}{G M^{2}} L_{G W}=-\frac{4 R^{2}}{G M^{2}} \frac{2 G^{4} M^{5}}{5 R^{5} c^{5}}$, giving $$ \frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{~d} t}=-\frac{8 G^{3} M^{3}}{5 R^{3} c^{5}} \quad(1 \text { point }) $$

question: In a binary neutron star system, two identical neutron stars of mass $M$ each undergo a circular orbit of radius $R$ around their center of mass. This problem explores the general relativistic effect of gravitational waves on this system, but the system can be approximated as Newtonian circular orbits which radiate energy but remain very nearly circular even though the radius is changing very slowly over time. Astronomers measure $R=0.750 \mathrm{AU}$ and the orbital period $P=387$ days. Calculate $M$, the mass of each neutron star, in solar masses.
answer: According to Kepler's Third Law, $G(M+m) P^{2}=4 \pi^{2} a^{3}$ (2 points), using the same variables as in the solution to part (b). Once again, $m=M$ and $a=2 R$ so $G M P^{2}=16 \pi^{2} R^{3}$ and $$ \begin{gathered} M=\frac{16 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G P^{2}}=\frac{16 \pi^{2}\left(0.750 \cdot 1.496 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~m}\right)^{3}}{\left(6.674 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~m}^{3} /\left(\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~s}^{2}\right)\right)(387 \cdot 24 \cdot 3600 \mathrm{~s})^{2}} \cdot \frac{1 M_{\odot}}{1.989 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{~kg}} M=1.50 M_{\odot}(\mathbf{1} \text { point }) . \end{gathered} $$

question: In a binary neutron star system, two identical neutron stars of mass $M$ each undergo a circular orbit of radius $R$ around their center of mass. This problem explores the general relativistic effect of gravitational waves on this system, but the system can be approximated as Newtonian circular orbits which radiate energy but remain very nearly circular even though the radius is changing very slowly over time. Verify the assumption that each orbit can be approximated as circular is valid by calculating the dimensionless parameter $\frac{\mathrm{d} R / \mathrm{d} t}{R / P}$ and commenting on what your calculated value means.
answer: $\frac{\mathrm{d} R / \mathrm{d} t}{R / P}$ is an approximation of the fractional change in the radius over one orbit, so its magnitude should be much less than one (and the sign negative because the orbit is shrinking) if each orbit is approximately circular; in other words, radius should be approximately constant over one orbit ( 2 points). $$ \begin{gathered} \frac{\mathrm{d} R / \mathrm{d} t}{R / P}=-\frac{8 G^{3} M^{3} P}{5 R^{4} c^{5}}=-\frac{8\left(6.674 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~m}^{3} /\left(\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~s}^{2}\right) \cdot 1.50 \cdot 1.989 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{~kg}\right)^{3}(387 \cdot 24 \cdot 3600 \mathrm{~s})}{5\left(0.750 \cdot 1.496 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~m}\right)^{4}\left(2.998 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right)^{5}} \frac{\mathrm{~d} R / \mathrm{d} t}{R / P}=-1.11 \times 10^{-18}(1 \text { point }) \end{gathered} $$ As expected, this is much smaller than one and therefore is consistent with the assumption we made.

question: In a binary neutron star system, two identical neutron stars of mass $M$ each undergo a circular orbit of radius $R$ around their center of mass. This problem explores the general relativistic effect of gravitational waves on this system, but the system can be approximated as Newtonian circular orbits which radiate energy but remain very nearly circular even though the radius is changing very slowly over time. In seconds and years, calculate $t_{m}$, the time until a merger between the two neutron stars, under the assumptions that the expression from part (b) is always true and that the merger occurs when $R=0$ since the radii of the neutron stars are negligible compared to the size of the orbit. Hint: $\int_{a}^{b} x^{\beta} \mathrm{d} x=\frac{1}{\beta+1}\left(b^{\beta+1}-a^{\beta+1}\right)$.
answer: From part (b), $$ \frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{~d} t}=-\frac{8 G^{3} M^{3}}{5 R^{3} c^{5}} $$ Separating the variables and integrating (1 point), we have \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{t_{m}} \mathrm{~d} t=t_{m}= & -\frac{5 c^{5}}{8 G^{3} M^{3}} \int_{R_{0}}^{0} R^{3} \mathrm{~d} R=\frac{5 c^{5}}{8 G^{3} M^{3}} \int_{0}^{R_{0}} R^{3} \mathrm{~d} R=\frac{5 c^{5} R_{0}^{4}}{32 G^{3} M^{3}}(2 \text { points }) t_{m} & =\frac{5\left(2.998 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right)^{5}\left(0.750 \cdot 1.496 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~m}\right)^{4}}{32\left(6.674 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~m}^{3} /\left(\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~s}^{2}\right) \cdot 1.50 \cdot 1.989 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{~kg}\right)^{3}} & =7.55 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~s} \cdot \frac{1 \text { year }}{365.2425 \cdot 24 \cdot 3600 \mathrm{~s}} \tag{1} & =2.39 \times 10^{17} \text { years }(1 \text { point }) \end{align*} This is much larger than the age of the universe, so clearly any neutron stars observed to collide must have started much closer than 1.5 AU!

question: You may attempt subsections without attempting the previous parts by making appropriate assumptions and justifying them. The famous Stupendous Man is on a trip from the headquarters of G.R.O.S.S., his base, to the hideous Shady Acres (a creepy housing development) to save the woods they are encroaching on. He travels on his Flying Carpet, which always takes the optimal path (shortest) between any two points on Earth. Stupendous Man is given the information that Shady Acres has a latitude of $23^{\circ}$ N. Meanwhile, he overhears that the headquarters of G.R.O.S.S. is also in the northern hemisphere, but does not know the specific latitude. Assume that the Tropic of Cancer resides at $23.5^{\circ} \mathrm{N}$. At some moment, Stupendous Man observes that the Flying Carpet is at a latitude of $50^{\circ} \mathrm{N}$ and is traveling exactly due West. Stupendous Man wonders if he is currently further North than the headquarters of G.R.O.S.S. Is it possible to reliably answer this question without any other information? If so, what is the answer? If not, explain why.
answer: We know that Stupendous Man is on the shortest possible path, which must be a great circle. Thus, if Stupendous Man is traveling exactly due West, then this must be the northernmost point in the trajectory of his flight, and thus he must be North of his starting point, as both destinations are in the Northern Hemisphere.

question: You may attempt subsections without attempting the previous parts by making appropriate assumptions and justifying them. The famous Stupendous Man is on a trip from the headquarters of G.R.O.S.S., his base, to the hideous Shady Acres (a creepy housing development) to save the woods they are encroaching on. He travels on his Flying Carpet, which always takes the optimal path (shortest) between any two points on Earth. Stupendous Man is given the information that Shady Acres has a latitude of $23^{\circ}$ N. Meanwhile, he overhears that the headquarters of G.R.O.S.S. is also in the northern hemisphere, but does not know the specific latitude. Assume that the Tropic of Cancer resides at $23.5^{\circ} \mathrm{N}$. ( $\mathbf{9}$ points) What portion of the rest of the flight path (from his current location to Shady Acres) lies above the Tropic of Cancer?
answer: The Tropic of Cancer is a latitude circle on Earth that is at around $23.5^{\circ}$ North of the Equator (A student may use a more accurate value, which will give a slightly different answer). Now, draw the arc connecting the North Pole of Earth (N) to Stupendous Man's current location (A), which we know must be the highest point in the great circle connecting G.R.O.S.S. and Shady Acres. It follows that $\angle \mathrm{BAN}=90^{\circ}$. (2 points) Note that this creates the spherical triangle $\triangle \mathrm{NBA}$ as seen in the figure. Next, draw the arc connecting N to the intersection point of the flight path and the Tropic of Cancer, call this point $T$. We are interested in the length of arc $A T$, which would give us the portion of the flight path that is above the Tropic of Cancer. To find the length of AT, we note that by construction, NA $=90^{\circ}-50^{\circ}=40^{\circ}$, NT $=$ $90^{\circ}-23.5^{\circ}=66.5^{\circ}$. Applying the cosine rule, we find that: $$ \begin{gathered} \cos (\mathrm{NT})=\cos (\mathrm{NA}) \cos (\mathrm{AT})+\sin (\mathrm{NA}) \sin (\mathrm{AT}) \cos \left(90^{\circ}\right) \Longrightarrow A T=58.63^{\circ} \end{gathered} $$ The portion of the flight path that is above the Tropic of Cancer must be AT/AB. To find AB , we note that $\mathrm{NB}=90^{\circ}-23^{\circ}=67^{\circ}$. Applying the cosine rule again, we have: $$ \begin{gathered} \cos (\mathrm{NB})=\cos (\mathrm{NA}) \cos (\mathrm{AB})+\sin (\mathrm{NA}) \sin (\mathrm{AB}) \cos \left(90^{\circ}\right) \Longrightarrow A B=59.33^{\circ} \end{gathered} $$ Thus, the answer is $\frac{58.63^{\circ}}{59.33^{\circ}}=0.988$.

To destroy Shady Acres, Stupendous Man needs to activate a device which can only be activated if the Sun is directly overhead (at the zenith). For what portion of the flight path would this be a possibility (the time of the year is unknown)?
answer: The highest declination that the Sun reaches over the course of the year is $23.5^{\circ} \mathrm{N}$ on the Summer Solstice. Thus, any portion of the path that lies below $23.5^{\circ}$ would have some time of the year where the Sun could be directly overhead. Thus, the answer is simply the complement to the answer of part b, which is 0.012 . (In other words, only places below this line can have 'zero shadow days'.)

question: You may attempt subsections without attempting the previous parts by making appropriate assumptions and justifying them. The famous Stupendous Man is on a trip from the headquarters of G.R.O.S.S., his base, to the hideous Shady Acres (a creepy housing development) to save the woods they are encroaching on. He travels on his Flying Carpet, which always takes the optimal path (shortest) between any two points on Earth. Stupendous Man is given the information that Shady Acres has a latitude of $23^{\circ}$ N. Meanwhile, he overhears that the headquarters of G.R.O.S.S. is also in the northern hemisphere, but does not know the specific latitude. Assume that the Tropic of Cancer resides at $23.5^{\circ} \mathrm{N}$. Some time later, it is June 21st and Stupendous Man is back at Shady Acres to show his partner, Hobbes, how successful his attack was. He wants to show Hobbes a great aerial view of the nature that has grown there since with an air balloon ride. He notices that the Sun is currently setting, giving rise to a beautiful view! To mesmerize Hobbes, Stupendous Man wants to keep the Sun at the horizon as they rise. Stupendous Man and Hobbes are in the air balloon currently 100 meters above the surface of the Earth. At this moment, what should be the instantaneous speed (in $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ ) of the balloon in order to keep up with the setting Sun (i.e. ensure that the Sun stays at their perceived horizon as it sets)? You may ignore the effects of atmospheric refraction. To help you, here are some rules of differentiation: $\frac{d}{d x}(\arccos x)=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ $\frac{d}{d x}\left(f(g(x))=\frac{d f}{d g} \frac{d g}{d x}\right.$ $\frac{d}{d x}\left(x^{n}\right)=n x^{n-1}$
answer: Since the balloon is traveling straight up, we first find the angular velocity of the Sun perpendicular to the horizon. Then we find an expression for the speed of the balloon and equate the two. Given that it is June 21st, we will assume that the current date is the date of the summer solstice. In particular, we know that $\delta_{\odot}=23.5^{\circ} \mathrm{N}$. Also, the Sun is moving in a small circle parallel to the Celestial Equator. The angular velocity of the Sun on the celestial sphere is $\omega_{c}=\frac{2 \pi}{24 * 60 * 60} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. For any declination of the Sun, the hour angle $H$ varies throughout the day at a constant rate of $\frac{d H}{d t}=\omega_{c}$. The next step is to obtain an expression for the rate of variation of the altitude $a$ of the Sun (which is equivalent to the angular velocity of the Sun perpendicular to the horizon) during the sunset as a function of $\delta_{\odot}, H$, and the latitude $\lambda$ : $$ \begin{aligned} \sin (a) & =\sin \left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \sin (\lambda)+\cos \left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \cos (\lambda) \cos (H) \frac{d}{d t} \sin (a) & =\frac{d}{d t}\left(\sin \left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \sin (\lambda)+\cos \left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \cos (\lambda) \cos (H)\right) \cos (a) \frac{d a}{d t} & =-\cos \left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \cos (\lambda) \sin (H) \frac{d H}{d t} \cos (a) \frac{d a}{d t} & =-\cos \left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \cos (\lambda) \sin (H) \omega_{c} \end{aligned} $$ During the sunset, $a=0^{\circ}$. It is also known that during the sunrise and the sunset, the following expression is valid: $\cos (H)=-\tan \left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \tan (\lambda)$. By the trigonometric identity $\sin ^{2} \theta+\cos ^{2} \theta=$ 1, it follows that $\sin (H)= \pm \sqrt{1-\tan ^{2}\left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \tan ^{2}(\lambda)}$. Since the Sun sets west of the local meridian, the hour angle must be in the ( $0 h, 12 h$ ) range, so its sine must be positive. Therefore, the final expression for the angular velocity of the Sun perpendicular to the horizon is the following: $$ \omega=\frac{d a}{d t}=-\cos \left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \cos (\lambda) \sqrt{1-\tan ^{2}\left(\delta_{\odot}\right) \tan ^{2}(\lambda)} \omega_{c}=-0.0000603 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} $$ The negative sign only indicates that the Sun is setting and not rising. Now, we find a relationship between the height the balloon is at $h$ and the angle below the horizon it can see $\theta$ (refer to the figure). We can see by angle chasing that $\angle A O D=\theta$ as well (both $\angle A D O$ and $\angle A B C$ are $90^{\circ}$. Since $A D O$ is a right angle triangle, we can say $$ \cos \theta=\frac{R_{E}}{R_{E}+h} $$ Note: on the version of the exam that was sent to the students, the first derivative on the provided list was incorrectly stated as $\frac{d}{d x}(\arccos x)=\frac{-1}{1-x^{2}}$ instead of $\frac{d}{d x}(\arccos x)=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$. This solution uses the correct expression for the derivative. When grading the exams, both solutions using the correct expression and the incorrect expression provided for this derivative were accepted. Say the velocity is $v$. We can differentiate the above expression with respect to time with the help of the formulas given and the chain rule. This is simplified as: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{d \theta}{d t} & =\frac{d}{d t}\left(\arccos \frac{R_{E}}{R_{E}+h}\right) & =\frac{d}{d h}\left(\arccos \frac{1}{1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}}\right) \cdot\left(\frac{d h}{d t}\right) & =\frac{d}{d h}\left(\arccos \frac{1}{1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}}\right) \cdot v & =\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}}\right)^{2}}} \cdot \frac{d}{d h}\left(\frac{1}{1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}}\right) \cdot v & =\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}}\right)^{2}}} \cdot \frac{-1}{\left(1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}\right)^{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{R_{E}} \cdot v & =\frac{v}{\frac{1}{1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}} \sqrt{\left(1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}\right)^{2}-1}\left(1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}\right)^{2} R_{E}} & =\frac{v}{\sqrt{1+2 \frac{h}{R_{E}}+\frac{h^{2}}{R_{E}^{2}}-1}\left(1+\frac{h}{R_{E}}\right) R_{E}} & =\frac{v}{\sqrt{2 \frac{h}{R_{E}}+\frac{h^{2}}{R_{E}^{2}}}\left(R_{E}+h\right)} \end{aligned} $$ Considering that $x \ll R_{E}$ : $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{d \theta}{d t} & \approx \frac{v}{\sqrt{2 \frac{h}{R_{E}} R_{E}}} & =\frac{v}{\sqrt{2 h R_{E}}} \end{aligned} $$ Finally, we equate $$ |\omega|=\left.\frac{d \theta}{d t}\right|_{h=100}=\frac{v}{\sqrt{2 h R_{E}}} $$ Solving for $v$, we get $v=2.15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

question: Spherical cluster A spherical star cluster, which appears from Earth under a solid angle of $4.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{sr}$, contains approximately $2 \times 10^{5}$ stars and has an apparent bolometric magnitude of $m_{\text {bol }}=5.8 \mathrm{mag}$. The spherical cluster is at rest, meaning the velocities of the stars are zero. Estimate the distance to the cluster as well as the mean angular separation between its stars. Ignore interstellar extinction. Also, compute the objective lens diameter of a telescope required to distinguish two stars of the cluster in the optical. State any assumptions you made.
answer: We start by assuming that all stars in the cluster are Sun-like, thus the total luminosity of the cluster is $L=N L_{\odot}=2 \times 10^{5} L_{\odot}$. Using Pogson's law we find the total absolute magnitude of the cluster: $$ M_{b o l}=M_{\odot}-2.5 \log \left(\frac{L}{L_{\odot}}\right)=4.8-2.5 \log \left(2 \times 10^{5}\right)=-8.45 $$ We apply distance modulus (ignoring extinction) to find the distance: $$ M_{b o l}-m_{b o l}=5-5 \log d $$ Solving for $d$ : $$ d=7100 \mathrm{pc} $$ The mean solid angle each star takes is calculated as: $$ \Omega_{\text {star }}=\frac{\Omega}{N}=\frac{4.5 \times 10^{-5}}{2 \times 10^{5}} \mathrm{sr} \approx 2.25 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{sr} $$ and thus, the corresponding angular separation is roughly: $$ \theta \approx \sqrt{2.25 \times 10^{-10}} \mathrm{rad}=1.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{rad}=3 \mathrm{arcsec} $$ Using the resolving power equation: $$ D=\frac{1.22 \lambda}{\theta} $$ Substituting values: $$ D=\frac{1.22 \times 500 \times 10^{-9}}{1.5 \times 10^{-5}} \mathrm{~m}=0.04 \mathrm{~m} $$

question: Spherical cluster A spherical star cluster, which appears from Earth under a solid angle of $4.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{sr}$, contains approximately $2 \times 10^{5}$ stars and has an apparent bolometric magnitude of $m_{\text {bol }}=5.8 \mathrm{mag}$. The spherical cluster is at rest, meaning the velocities of the stars are zero. Suppose the cluster undergoes gravitational contraction, which stops when it reaches a state where the virial theorem holds. Find the new radius of the cluster as a function of its initial radius and compute its numerical value.
answer: We first calculate the cluster's initial radius using the definition of solid angle for a sphere: $$ \Omega=\frac{\pi R_{i}^{2}}{d^{2}} $$ which gives $$ R_{i}=8.3 \times 10^{17} \mathrm{~m}=26.9 \mathrm{pc} $$ The velocities of stars are initially zero, hence the initial mechanic energy of the cluster is solely its gravitational potential energy: $$ E_{i}=U_{i}=-\frac{3}{5} \frac{G M^{2}}{R_{i}} $$ After the contraction the total energy is given by: $$ E_{f}=K_{f}+U_{f} $$ but the virial theorem also applies: $$ 2 K_{f}+U_{f}=0 $$ hence, $$ E_{f}=\frac{U_{f}}{2}=-\frac{3}{10} \frac{G M^{2}}{R_{f}} $$ By conservation of energy: $$ E_{i}=E_{f} $$ we find $$ R_{f}=\frac{R_{i}}{2}=\frac{26.9 \mathrm{pc}}{2}=13.5 \mathrm{pc} $$

question: Spherical cluster A spherical star cluster, which appears from Earth under a solid angle of $4.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{sr}$, contains approximately $2 \times 10^{5}$ stars and has an apparent bolometric magnitude of $m_{\text {bol }}=5.8 \mathrm{mag}$. The spherical cluster is at rest, meaning the velocities of the stars are zero. Calculate the mean time $(\tau)$ between two successive stellar collisions as a function of the mean mass of a star in the cluster ( $m$ ), their relative velocity ( $v$ ), the numerical density of stars $(n)$, and any other parameters you might need. Perform a numerical substitution to find the time $\tau$, after estimating $v$ and $n$. We define $X, Y, Z$ as the mass fractions of a star (and consequently a cluster) consisting of hydrogen, helium, and metals (elements heavier than H and He in astrophysics), respectively. Specifically, $Z$ is called the metallicity, and it is given by the relation: $$ Z=\sum_{i>\mathrm{He}} \frac{m_{i}}{m_{\text {total }}} $$
answer: For two stars to collide, they should be bound (negative energy), thus $$ \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}<\frac{G m m}{r} $$ which implies: $$ r<\frac{2 G m}{v^{2}} $$ The time $\tau$ is given by: $$ \tau=\frac{\ell}{v} $$ where $\ell$ is the mean free path. $$ \ell=\frac{1}{n \pi r^{2}}=\frac{v^{4}}{4 \pi G^{2} n m^{2}} $$ Thus the time between stellar collisions is given by, $$ \tau=\frac{v^{3}}{4 \pi G^{2} n m^{2}} $$ Credit should also be given if students arrive at a similar expression/follow a different approach. An acceptable solution is: $$ \tau=\frac{v}{\pi G n m R_{\text {star }}} $$ in which case $R_{\text {star }}$ refers to the radius of a typical star. One would get it taking $r$ in the mean free path calculation to be the effective collision radius in the limit of large $v$ (see solution to Problem 7a, the derivation follows similarly). From the virial theorem: $$ \begin{gathered} 2 K+U=0 2 \times \frac{1}{2} M v^{2}=\frac{3}{5} \frac{G M^{2}}{R} v=\sqrt{\frac{3 G M}{5 R}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 G N m}{5 R}} \end{gathered} $$ and $$ n=\frac{N}{V}=\frac{3 N}{4 \pi R_{f}^{3}} $$ From numerical substitution $\left(m=M_{\odot}\right)$ : $$ \tau \approx 1.3 \mathrm{Gyr} $$

question: Spherical cluster A spherical star cluster, which appears from Earth under a solid angle of $4.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{sr}$, contains approximately $2 \times 10^{5}$ stars and has an apparent bolometric magnitude of $m_{\text {bol }}=5.8 \mathrm{mag}$. The spherical cluster is at rest, meaning the velocities of the stars are zero. First, relate $X, Y, Z$ and compute the mean molecular weight of the Sun. Given are the atomic and mass numbers of ${ }^{1} H,{ }^{4} H e$, and metals and you may assume the mass number is approximately twice the atomic number for metals. For the Sun, we have $X_{\odot}=0.739, Z_{\odot}=0.012$. Of particular interest for determining the age of a cluster is the quantity: $$ \left[\frac{F e}{H}\right] \equiv \log \left(\frac{\left(N_{F e} / N_{H}\right)_{\text {cluster }}}{\left(N_{F e} / N_{H}\right)_{\odot}}\right), $$ where the notation $N_{F e}, N_{H}$ represents the number densities of iron ( Fe ) and hydrogen (H), respectively.
answer: Given $X+Y+Z=1$, and using the values: $$ X_{\odot}=0.739, \quad Z_{\odot}=0.012 $$ we get $$ Y_{\odot}=1-X_{\odot}-Z_{\odot}=0.249 $$ The mean molecular weight is given by the relation: $$ \mu=\frac{A}{Z+1} $$ For different components: $$ \begin{gathered} \mu_{H}=\frac{1}{1+1}=\frac{1}{2} \mu_{H e}=\frac{4}{2+2}=\frac{4}{3} \mu_{m}=\frac{A_{m}}{Z_{m}+1} \approx \frac{A_{m}}{Z_{m}} \approx \frac{2 Z_{m}}{Z_{m}}=2 \end{gathered} $$ Thus, the total mean molecular weight is: $$ \mu=\frac{1}{2 X+\frac{3 Y}{4}+\frac{Z}{2}} $$ and for the Sun: $$ \mu=\frac{1}{2 X_{\odot}+\frac{3 Y_{\odot}}{4}+\frac{Z_{\odot}}{2}}=0.598 $$

question: Spherical cluster A spherical star cluster, which appears from Earth under a solid angle of $4.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{sr}$, contains approximately $2 \times 10^{5}$ stars and has an apparent bolometric magnitude of $m_{\text {bol }}=5.8 \mathrm{mag}$. The spherical cluster is at rest, meaning the velocities of the stars are zero. If the cluster has $[F e / H]=-2.53 \mathrm{dex}$, find the ratio $\left(N_{F e} / N_{H}\right)_{\text {cluster }}$. What does the negative sign in $[F e / H]$ indicate?
answer: We have $$ \frac{N_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{N_{\mathrm{H}}}=\frac{Z_{\odot}}{X_{\odot}}=\frac{0.012}{0.739}=0.016 $$ and $$ \left[\frac{\mathrm{Fe}}{\mathrm{H}}\right]=\log \left(\frac{\left(N_{\mathrm{Fe}} / N_{\mathrm{H}}\right)_{\text {cluster }}}{\left(N_{\mathrm{Fe}} / N_{\mathrm{H}}\right)_{\odot}}\right)=\left(\left(N_{\mathrm{Fe}} / N_{\mathrm{H}}\right)_{\text {cluster }}\right)-(-1.79) $$ thus $$ \left(\frac{N_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{N_{\mathrm{H}}}\right)_{\text {cluster }}=8.6 \times 10^{-8} $$ A negative value of $[\mathrm{Fe} / \mathrm{H}]$ suggests that the cluster is more metal-poor than the Sun.

question: Planetary Defense Oh no! Asteroid B612 is on a collision course with the Earth. Its relevant orbital and physical parameters are as follows: Parameter & Value Semi-major axis $a$ & 2.00 AU Eccentricity $e$ & 0.50 Inclination $i$ & $10.0^{\circ}$ Argument of perihelion $\omega$ & $0^{\circ}$ Mass $m \quad 6.40 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~kg}$ The orbit is shown in the diagram (not to scale). B612's orbit crosses Earth's orbit at B612's perihelion. B612 is currently at its aphelion, and is on a course to impact Earth at B612's next perihelion, half an orbit from now. Specifically, its trajectory puts it on a course to precisely intersect the center of the Earth (if it could pass through the surface). Assume for all parts that Earth is on a circular orbit with zero inclination. The effect of Earth's gravity can make this problem tricky. But there is a useful simplification that you can make. Consider an asteroid that is approaching Earth at relative velocity $v$. If unperturbed by Earth's gravity, it would pass a distance $b$ from the Earth's center ( $b$ is known as the impact parameter). In the presence of Earth's gravity, this trajectory might be deflected so that the asteroid impacts Earth, even if $b$ is larger than $R_{\oplus}$ (see diagram.) The largest $b$ such that the asteroid impacts Earth is called $R_{\text {eff }}$, the effective collision radius. Find an expression for $R_{\text {eff }}$. What are $v$ and $R_{\text {eff }}$ for B612's approach? Once we have calculated $R_{\text {eff }}$, we can ignore Earth's gravity for the remaining parts by just assuming there will be an impact if $b<R_{\text {eff }}$.
answer: One approach is to use conservation of angular momentum and conservation of energy. If $b=R_{\text {eff }}$, then on its perturbed trajectory, the asteroid should just skim the surface of the Earth (at distance $R_{\oplus}$ from Earth's center). Let's call the velocity at that point $v_{s}$. The asteroid's angular momentum when it first enters Earth's gravity well is $v R_{\text {eff }}$. Conservation of angular momentum says that $$ v_{s} R_{\oplus}=v R_{\mathrm{eff}} $$ When the asteroid skims the Earth, it has gravitational potential energy $-\frac{G m M_{\oplus}}{R_{\oplus}}$. When it first enters Earth's gravity well, its gravitational potential energy is (asymptotically) zero. Conservation of energy therefore says that $$ \frac{1}{2} m v_{s}^{2}-\frac{G m M_{\oplus}}{R_{\oplus}}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} $$ Putting these together, we can solve for $v_{s}$ and $R_{\text {eff }}$ in terms of known parameters, giving: $$ R_{\mathrm{eff}}=R_{\oplus} \sqrt{1+\frac{2 G M_{\oplus}}{R_{\oplus} v^{2}}} $$ Intuitively, $R_{\text {eff }}$ will always be greater than or equal to $R_{\oplus}$, and is larger for smaller $v$ since slower-moving asteroids are deflected more strongly. Now we need to calculate $v$ and $R_{\text {eff }}$ for this specific case. Let's shift to the Sun's reference frame. At perihelion, B612's velocity is $$ v_{p}=\sqrt{G M_{\odot}\left(\frac{2}{1 \mathrm{AU}}-\frac{1}{2 \mathrm{AU}}\right)}=36.5 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s} $$ This is angled $10^{\circ}$ with respect to the Earth's velocity, $$ v_{\oplus}=\sqrt{\frac{G M_{\odot}}{1 \mathrm{AU}}}=29.8 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s} $$ From here, we just have to subtract the two vectors to get the relative velocity. $$ v=\left|\vec{v}_{a}-\vec{v}_{\oplus}\right|=\sqrt{v_{a}^{2}+v_{\oplus}^{2}-2 v_{a} v_{\oplus} \cos \left(10^{\circ}\right)}=8.8 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s} $$ Plugging this in to the formula we obtained for $R_{\text {eff }}$ gives $$ R_{\mathrm{eff}}=1.61 R_{\oplus}=1.03 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~km} $$ From here on out, we will completely ignore the effect of Earth's gravity and instead pretend like the radius of the Earth is $R_{\text {eff }}$.
caption: Gravitational focusing diagram defining the asteroid's impact parameter and effective collision radius.

question: Planetary Defense Oh no! Asteroid B612 is on a collision course with the Earth. Its relevant orbital and physical parameters are as follows: Parameter & Value Semi-major axis $a$ & 2.00 AU Eccentricity $e$ & 0.50 Inclination $i$ & $10.0^{\circ}$ Argument of perihelion $\omega$ & $0^{\circ}$ Mass $m \quad 6.40 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~kg}$ The orbit is shown in the diagram (not to scale). B612's orbit crosses Earth's orbit at B612's perihelion. B612 is currently at its aphelion, and is on a course to impact Earth at B612's next perihelion, half an orbit from now. Specifically, its trajectory puts it on a course to precisely intersect the center of the Earth (if it could pass through the surface). Assume for all parts that Earth is on a circular orbit with zero inclination. ( $\mathbf{5}$ points) If B612 were to hit Earth, what would be the kinetic energy of the collision? For comparison, a typical nuclear explosion has an energy of around $10^{15}$ to $10^{16} \mathrm{~J}$. Thankfully, a spacecraft similar to the 2022 Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission has just arrived at B612 to impact it at high speed and deflect its trajectory away from Earth. For the rest of this problem, we will determine whether this mission can succeed.
answer: Note that the impact velocity is not the $v$ that we calculated in the previous part - it's actually $v_{s}$, since B612 picks up speed as it falls into Earth's gravity well. The kinetic energy at impact is $E=\frac{1}{2} m v_{s}^{2}$. As we found in part (a), $\frac{1}{2} m v_{s}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}+\frac{G m M_{\oplus}}{R_{\oplus}}$. Plugging in the value of $v$ from part (a) and the given value of $m=6.4 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~kg}$, we get $$ E=6.5 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{~J} $$ Comparable to a large nuclear bomb! This asteroid is not large enough to destroy human civilization, but would be a major threat if it were to hit a populated area.
caption: Diagram of B612's inclined orbit crossing Earth's orbit at perihelion.

question: Planetary Defense Oh no! Asteroid B612 is on a collision course with the Earth. Its relevant orbital and physical parameters are as follows: Parameter & Value Semi-major axis $a$ & 2.00 AU Eccentricity $e$ & 0.50 Inclination $i$ & $10.0^{\circ}$ Argument of perihelion $\omega$ & $0^{\circ}$ Mass $m \quad 6.40 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~kg}$ The orbit is shown in the diagram (not to scale). B612's orbit crosses Earth's orbit at B612's perihelion. B612 is currently at its aphelion, and is on a course to impact Earth at B612's next perihelion, half an orbit from now. Specifically, its trajectory puts it on a course to precisely intersect the center of the Earth (if it could pass through the surface). Assume for all parts that Earth is on a circular orbit with zero inclination. The kinetic deflector is similar to DART, with a moderate upgrade to mass and speed. It has a mass of 2000 kg and will impact B612 with a relative velocity of $10 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}$. DART observed a momentum transfer of about $4 \times$ what would be expected from a fully inelastic collision, due to recoil from ejecta produced by the collision. Assume this collision will have the same $4 \times$ enhancement. How much of a change in velocity $(\Delta v)$ can we expect to impart with this kinetic deflector?
answer: In a fully inelastic collision, the two bodies stick together and momentum is conserved: $$ m_{1} v_{1}+m_{2} v_{2}=\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right) v_{f} $$ Take $m_{1}$ to be the spacecraft and $m_{2}$ to be $\mathrm{B} 612\left(m_{2} \gg m_{1}\right)$. In B612's frame $v_{2}=0$ so we have $$ m_{1} v_{1}=m_{2} v_{f} $$ Using the given values of $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $v_{1}$, we have $v_{f}=3.1 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$. If the actual momentum transfer is 4 times larger, then we can achieve a $\Delta v$ of $12.5 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$.

question: Planetary Defense Oh no! Asteroid B612 is on a collision course with the Earth. Its relevant orbital and physical parameters are as follows: Parameter & Value Semi-major axis $a$ & 2.00 AU Eccentricity $e$ & 0.50 Inclination $i$ & $10.0^{\circ}$ Argument of perihelion $\omega$ & $0^{\circ}$ Mass $m \quad 6.40 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~kg}$ The orbit is shown in the diagram (not to scale). B612's orbit crosses Earth's orbit at B612's perihelion. B612 is currently at its aphelion, and is on a course to impact Earth at B612's next perihelion, half an orbit from now. Specifically, its trajectory puts it on a course to precisely intersect the center of the Earth (if it could pass through the surface). Assume for all parts that Earth is on a circular orbit with zero inclination. ( $\mathbf{5}$ points) Make the (completely unrealistic) assumption that the kinetic deflector can hit B612 in any direction, and the achievable impact velocity is independent of the direction. What direction(s) would be most effective for deflecting B612 away from the Earth? Justify your reasoning, though you don't need to prove it rigorously. Given everything you found in parts (a) through (d), we will now determine whether it is possible to deflect B612 so that it misses Earth. Denote the point in the heliocentric reference frame where B612's and Earth's orbits intersect as point $P$, and the time of the collision at $t$ (when B612 and Earth are both at point $P$ ). It is highly recommended that you draw a picture for the remaining parts.
answer: The most efficient approach is to impact B612 along (or against) the direction of its motion around the Sun. We can think about this in terms of the change to B612's kinetic energy: hitting it along its direction of motion changes the kinetic energy by much more than hitting it perpendicularly to its direction of motion. Also, hitting it perpendicularly to its direction of motion does not change the orbital angular momentum. Another way to think about this, which I won't prove, is that a small kick along either of the other two axes won't change the position or timing of perihelion to first order. One or both of these things must be changed in order to deflect B612 away from Earth. In fact, this isn't specific to the configuration in the problem - unless an asteroid is on its final approach to Earth, hitting along the direction of motion is generally the most efficient way to deflect it.
caption: Diagram of B612's inclined orbit crossing Earth's orbit at perihelion.

question: Planetary Defense Oh no! Asteroid B612 is on a collision course with the Earth. Its relevant orbital and physical parameters are as follows: Parameter & Value Semi-major axis $a$ & 2.00 AU Eccentricity $e$ & 0.50 Inclination $i$ & $10.0^{\circ}$ Argument of perihelion $\omega$ & $0^{\circ}$ Mass $m \quad 6.40 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~kg}$ The orbit is shown in the diagram (not to scale). B612's orbit crosses Earth's orbit at B612's perihelion. B612 is currently at its aphelion, and is on a course to impact Earth at B612's next perihelion, half an orbit from now. Specifically, its trajectory puts it on a course to precisely intersect the center of the Earth (if it could pass through the surface). Assume for all parts that Earth is on a circular orbit with zero inclination. Before the deflection (which occurs at B612's aphelion), the perihelion of B612's orbit is at point $P$. After the deflection, the new perihelion is at point $P^{\prime}$. What is the distance between $P^{\prime}$ and $P$ ? Is this distance on its own enough for B612 to miss the Earth? Hint: We are doing small perturbations, so make use of first-order Taylor expansions!
answer: If the perihelion and aphelion distances are $r_{p}$ and $r_{a}$ respectively, we have $a=\frac{r_{p}+r_{a}}{2}$. Note that the perturbation can't change $r_{a}$, since B 612 is at its aphelion right now. Thus we can treat $r_{a}=3 \mathrm{AU}$ as constant. The velocity at aphelion is $v_{a}$. The vis-viva equation says that $$ v_{a}^{2}=G M_{\odot}\left(\frac{2}{r}-\frac{1}{a}\right)=G M_{\odot}\left(\frac{2}{r_{a}}-\frac{2}{r_{p}+r_{a}}\right) $$ We can solve for $v_{a}$ to get $v_{a}=12.2 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}$. We can also invert the vis-viva equation to isolate $r_{p}$ : $$ r_{p}=\frac{r_{a}^{2} v_{a}^{2}}{2 G M_{\odot}-r_{a} v_{a}^{2}} $$ and take the derivative to get $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{d r_{p}}{d v_{a}} & =\frac{4 G M_{\odot} r_{a}^{2} v_{a}}{\left(2 G M_{\odot}-r_{a} v_{a}^{2}\right)^{2}} & =\frac{8}{9} \frac{r_{a}}{v_{a}} \end{aligned} $$ An alternative approach is to obtain from the vis-viva equation $$ \begin{aligned} 2 v_{a} \frac{d v_{a}}{d r_{p}} & =\frac{v_{a}^{2} r_{a}}{r_{p}^{2}+r_{a} r_{p}} & =\frac{9}{4} \frac{v_{a}^{2}}{r_{a}} \end{aligned} $$ Finally a first-order expansion using the result of (c) gives $$ \Delta r_{p} \approx \frac{d r_{p}}{d v_{a}} \Delta v_{a}=4.10 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~km}=0.40 R_{\mathrm{eff}} $$ This is not far enough!
caption: Diagram of B612's inclined orbit crossing Earth's orbit at perihelion.

question: Planetary Defense Oh no! Asteroid B612 is on a collision course with the Earth. Its relevant orbital and physical parameters are as follows: Parameter & Value Semi-major axis $a$ & 2.00 AU Eccentricity $e$ & 0.50 Inclination $i$ & $10.0^{\circ}$ Argument of perihelion $\omega$ & $0^{\circ}$ Mass $m \quad 6.40 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~kg}$ The orbit is shown in the diagram (not to scale). B612's orbit crosses Earth's orbit at B612's perihelion. B612 is currently at its aphelion, and is on a course to impact Earth at B612's next perihelion, half an orbit from now. Specifically, its trajectory puts it on a course to precisely intersect the center of the Earth (if it could pass through the surface). Assume for all parts that Earth is on a circular orbit with zero inclination. ( $\mathbf{5}$ points) After the deflection, B612 reaches point $P^{\prime}$ at time $t^{\prime}$. What is $\left|t^{\prime}-t\right|$ ? Knowing that Earth still reaches point $P$ at time $t$, how far is Earth from point $P$ at time $t^{\prime}$ ?
answer: All hope is not lost, however. The deflection won't just change the distance between Earth's and B612's orbits, but also the relative timing for B612 and Earth to pass the orbit intersection point. If the orbital period $T$ of B612 changes by $\Delta T$, then the time at which it crosses Earth's orbit (the next perihelion) changes by $\frac{\Delta T}{2}$. There are several ways to calculate $\Delta T$, but we'll take advantage of the fact that we already calculated $\Delta r_{p}$. Kepler's third law says that $T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{a^{3}}{G M_{\odot}}}$, or 2.83 years for B612. If we differentiate with respect to $a$, we get $$ \frac{d T}{d a}=\frac{3 T}{2 a} $$ Using the chain rule: $$ \frac{d T}{d r_{p}}=\frac{d T}{d a} \frac{d a}{d r_{p}}=\frac{3 T}{4 a} $$ We can use this to do another first-order expansion: $$ \Delta T \approx \frac{d T}{d r_{p}} \Delta r_{p}=15.3 \mathrm{~min} $$ The change in the perihelion time $\left|t-t^{\prime}\right|$ is half of the change in the orbital period, or $\frac{\Delta T}{2}=$ 7.6 min . In 7.6 min , the Earth travels a distance $2 \pi \mathrm{AU} \times \frac{7.6 \mathrm{~min}}{1 \text { year }}=1.37 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~km}$ along its orbit. Thus, at time $t^{\prime}$ the Earth is $1.37 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~km}$ away from point $P$. Let's call this distance $d_{\oplus}$.

Its relevant orbital and physical parameters are as follows: Parameter & Value Semi-major axis $a$ & 2.00 AU Eccentricity $e$ & 0.50 Inclination $i$ & $10.0^{\circ}$ Argument of perihelion $\omega$ & $0^{\circ}$ Mass $m \quad 6.40 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~kg}$ The orbit is shown in the diagram (not to scale). B612's orbit crosses Earth's orbit at B612's perihelion. B612 is currently at its aphelion, and is on a course to impact Earth at B612's next perihelion, half an orbit from now. Specifically, its trajectory puts it on a course to precisely intersect the center of the Earth (if it could pass through the surface). Assume for all parts that Earth is on a circular orbit with zero inclination. Shift to a reference frame where Earth is at rest as B612 passes by. As seen in this reference frame, what is the angle between B612's trajectory and the ecliptic plane as B612 is approaching Earth? Hint: It's not $10^{\circ}$.
answer: We have to be extremely careful for this next part. It is helpful to shift into Earth's reference frame, and think about the approach trajectory that B612 takes as seen from Earth. In this reference frame, the angle $\theta$ between the Earth's orbit and B612's trajectory as it passes by Earth is the angle of the relative velocity vector calculated in (a), which can be obtained from the law of sines: $$ \begin{gathered} \sin \theta=\sin \left(10^{\circ}\right) \frac{36.5 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}}{8.8 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}} \theta=46^{\circ} \end{gathered} $$ Note that this is much larger than the inclination of $10^{\circ}$, because the Earth's motion cancels some of B612's motion along the direction of Earth's orbit.

question: Planetary Defense Oh no! Asteroid B612 is on a collision course with the Earth. Its relevant orbital and physical parameters are as follows: Parameter & Value Semi-major axis $a$ & 2.00 AU Eccentricity $e$ & 0.50 Inclination $i$ & $10.0^{\circ}$ Argument of perihelion $\omega$ & $0^{\circ}$ Mass $m \quad 6.40 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~kg}$ The orbit is shown in the diagram (not to scale). B612's orbit crosses Earth's orbit at B612's perihelion. B612 is currently at its aphelion, and is on a course to impact Earth at B612's next perihelion, half an orbit from now. Specifically, its trajectory puts it on a course to precisely intersect the center of the Earth (if it could pass through the surface). Assume for all parts that Earth is on a circular orbit with zero inclination. After the deflection, what is the minimum approach distance $d$ of B612 to Earth? Hints: The closest approach does not occur at time $t^{\prime}$. Keep using the reference frame from part (g). It makes this part much easier as well. You will need all the results you got in parts (e) through (g). How does this compare to $R_{\text {eff }}$ ? Is the deflection successful?
answer: If the deflection puts Earth a distance $d_{\oplus}$ away from point $P$ when B612 crosses point $P^{\prime}$, then we can think of B612's trajectory in the Earth's reference frame as being shifted by a distance $d_{\oplus}$ away from Earth along the direction of Earth's orbit. The minimum approach distance is attained whenever the line from B612 to Earth is perpendicular to this trajectory. Thus, the actual closest approach (in the plane perpendicular to the ecliptic plane and tangent to Earth's orbit) is $d_{\perp}=d_{\oplus} \sin \theta$ (to understand why, it might help to see the diagram). Therefore, we want $d_{\oplus} \sin \theta>R_{\text {eff }}$ for a successful deflection. Note that we calculated $d_{\oplus}$ in part (f). Unfortunately, the closest approach is $$ d_{\perp}=d_{\oplus} \sin \theta=9.86 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~km}=0.96 R_{\mathrm{eff}} $$ which is still not quite far enough! But we should remember from part (e) that the orbit of B612 was also shifted a distance of $\Delta r_{p}$ radially. Thus, the true minimum approach distance (the impact parameter) is actually the hypotenuse of a right triangle: $$ b=\sqrt{d_{\perp}^{2}+\left(\Delta r_{p}\right)^{2}}=1.06 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~km}=1.03 R_{\mathrm{eff}} $$ which is just baaarely far enough for B612 to miss the Earth! The mission is successful. The following figure (not to scale) visually shows the geometry of this solution. It might look a little bit strange that Earth's orbit is shown despite the fact that we are in Earth's reference frame - think of it as just serving to define the coordinate system. In this frame, Earth really is staying still as B612 passes by. As a final note, deflecting an asteroid at perihelion is much more efficient than doing it at aphelion due to the Oberth effect. But in real life, we might not detect the asteroid far enough in advance to have the chance to deflect it at perihelion. Also, doing it at aphelion makes the problem more interesting!
